claims.text: Reported progress numbers measure different things: one AI-assisted Super Mario 64 DS project reports 99.9% of functions matched while its readable-source conversion counter sits at 30.5%. Likewise, decomp.dev separates a 'decompiled' percentage from a 'fully linked' one, so a single completion figure can overstate real, shippable status.

claims.text: A matching decompilation only proves one specific compiler turns the C into the original bytes, not that the C means the same thing to another compiler or ABI. In the V-Rally port, a set of matched functions each behaved wrongly once built for another target, including cars starting backwards, textures loading at 0 by 0 pixels and sign errors turning 255 into -1. Any name or semantics inferred from a match should be treated as unverified until run under a different build.

meta.capability: You can stop treating a byte-for-byte match as proof that a function's imported name or behavior is correct, and budget separate behavioral checks before trusting matched code.

claims.text: The sources point to cheap behavior checks that surface errors a match hides: building under a second modern compiler, building a port, and comparing memory against the running original. Super Mario 64 already runs a host GCC syntax check alongside the IDO build, and every bug on the V-Rally page was found by building a port. A progress percentage from a match checker is not a correctness measure.

claims.text: When several static libraries bundled into one product carry duplicated code, the application gets materially larger, and the same duplication is what produces naming collisions and unpredictable crashes. Duplicate copies of the same library are therefore a recurring, avoidable cost, not just a technical curiosity.

claims.text: In an unlinked object file, references to other functions and to global data are left as unresolved placeholders listed in a relocation table, and the linker computes the real addresses only afterward. So two identical functions can differ in bytes at exactly those reference sites depending on where the linker places things, which means a comparison must account for relocation entries rather than raw bytes alone.

meta.query: Why do two copies of the same function compiled by the Metrowerks compiler end up with different bytes, and how do relocations, register allocation, inlining and linker-generated stubs change what a matcher sees?
meta.capability: You can stop treating byte differences between two compiled copies of the same function as proof the source differs, and expect address-dependent bytes to be placeholders the linker fills in later.

claims.text: A call to a function in another module is compiled as a call to a small jump stub, which loads the real target through a table that is resolved lazily. The stub and table are generated at link time, so the code inside the function looks ordinary while the stub it lands on differs by link layout.

meta.capability: You can expect calls to external functions to appear as calls to linker-generated stubs, so a mismatch at a call site may come from the stub layer rather than from the function being compared.

claims.text: CodeWarrior exposes many code-generation controls: the pragma list in the reference includes scheduling, peephole, register_coloring, optimization_level, optimize_for_size, and PPC loop-unrolling limits. The profiler option additionally inserts compiler-generated code at the entry and exit of every profiled routine. Each of these can alter emitted instructions independently of the compiler version, so any comparison needs to fix them.

claims.text: CodeWarrior shipped about eleven numbered releases from December 1993 to December 1996, plus later Pro releases, so many compiler builds exist to match against. Its PPC code generator was written from scratch around Chaitin-style register allocation, and the later pragma list shows additional PPC unrolling controls. This suggests version-to-version differences in register allocation and scheduling are plausible, though no content measures them.

claims.text: When a branch target is out of range, the instruction encoding is already fixed at link time, so the linker cannot change it. Instead it generates a thunk (also called a veneer, branch stub, or trampoline) and redirects the original branch to it. The linked binary therefore contains extra linker-made code that never existed in the compiler's output, and the call site now points at the thunk rather than the real callee. A matching tool comparing linked bytes against compiled objects will see mismatches that are not compiler differences.

meta.query: Why does the Metrowerks linker sometimes insert branch stubs or veneers or rewrite relocated addresses, and what happens to the bytes a matching tool compares when it does?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming a linked binary's bytes mirror the compiled object, and treat any byte-level match against a compiler's raw output as valid only before linking, since the linker can add code or rewrite call targets afterward.

claims.text: The mwcc-rs project defines parity as emitting the same relocatable object as the real Metrowerks compiler, byte for byte, and treats an exact .text section alone as useful evidence but not parity. It also keys on section ordering, symbol order, alignment, and relocations such as R_PPC_EMB_SDA21. Comparing at the object stage, before addresses are assigned, avoids layout-dependent changes made at link time.

meta.query: Why does the Metrowerks linker sometimes insert branch stubs or veneers or rewrite relocated addresses, and what happens to the bytes a matching tool compares when it does?
meta.capability: You can decide to run byte-exact verification on relocatable object files, where the compiler's output is authoritative, instead of on final linked images, which cuts out linker-induced noise.

claims.text: A relocation table lists addresses in the object code that must be changed once final locations are assigned, and the linker modifies symbol references in code and data to point at the assigned run-time addresses. Bytes at those positions differ between the object and the linked image by design. A comparison tool therefore has to treat these fields as relocations, not as literal bytes.

meta.capability: You can expect that, for a given target, relocation-bearing instructions in an object hold placeholder values the linker overwrites, so a matching tool must mask or compare them by relocation entry rather than by raw bytes.

claims.text: Compiler version changes can alter struct layout, calling conventions and virtual table layout, and the standard library's own layout (e.g. std::string after C++11) differs between versions. Code compiled by different toolchain versions therefore has different machine-level shape, so a signature database built from one toolchain will see the same source function as different bytes and may miss it or misattribute it.

A matched function name therefore does not guarantee the same behavior or body as the reference, which raises the risk of a confident but wrong identification.

claims.text: Shared libraries such as glibc keep multiple versioned implementations of the same function, for example memcpy@GLIBC_2.2.5 alongside memcpy@@GLIBC_2.14, and binaries built years apart bind to different ones. Matching must therefore cover every retained variant, and a database that stores only the newest will miss or mislabel older builds.

claims.text: When every call to a function is inlined and its address is never taken, the compiler emits no standalone copy of that function at all, so a signature built from the standalone version has nothing to match. A 'not found' result can therefore mean the code is present but dissolved into its callers, not that the library was never used.

claims.text: Inlining puts a separate copy of the function body at each call site, and then optimizes each copy in its caller's context. Constants passed in can fold away branches, so no two copies need look alike or look like the standalone function. A signature may match some copies, none, or fire inconsistently, and an inlined function called 10 times yields 10 differing copies instead of one.

Game-specific naming came from strings, imports, and accidental debug leftovers: Devilution used a symbols file left on the Japanese PlayStation disc plus a debug build hidden in the PC data archives, and Silent Hill's team had to reverse-engineer an undocumented internal Konami vibration library by hand. Signature fingerprinting therefore does not reach proprietary engine code.

claims.text: In SBridge's evaluation, optimization level was the largest single driver of match reliability: top-1 recall was 84.96% at -O0 versus 65.31% at -O2, while architecture (about 71-78%) and compiler (GCC 75.4% vs Clang 74.9%) barely moved it. Binaries built with heavy optimization should therefore be treated as lower-confidence matches regardless of platform or compiler.
